mcqs.question: A team wants every version change to be immediately visible in server logs and easy to route without inspecting request headers. Which versioning approach fits that requirement best?
options: URI versioning, e.g. /v2/orders — the version is visible in the URL itself, including in logs
Header versioning — the version lives in an Accept header instead of the URL
No versioning at all, with only backward-compatible changes ever made
Versioning via a request body field instead of the URL or headers
mcqs.explanation: URI versioning puts the version directly in the path, so it shows up in access logs, bookmarks, and routing rules without needing to inspect headers or bodies. Header versioning is precisely the approach that's invisible without extra inspection; no versioning avoids the visibility question entirely but requires strict discipline; a body field doesn't help with routing before the body is even parsed.

mcqs.question: Which of these changes to an existing API endpoint is backward-compatible (safe, no version bump needed)?
options: Renaming a response field from user_name to name
Adding a new optional field to the response that existing clients simply won't read
Changing a field's type from string to integer
Making a previously-optional request field required
mcqs.explanation: Adding a new field that old clients weren't reading is the textbook safe, additive change — nothing that already worked stops working. Renaming a field, changing its type, or tightening optional-to-required are all classic breaking changes: each one changes behavior for a client that was relying on the old contract as documented.

mcqs.question: A team changes a response field's type from a string "19.99" to a number 19.99, reasoning that the value is 'basically the same' and ships it without a version bump. What's the actual risk?
options: There's no real risk since the numeric value is unchanged
The risk only applies to fields representing currency, not other numeric fields
A client's code expecting a string (e.g. calling .split() or a string-typed parser) can throw or silently misbehave the instant the field's type changes
This is safe as long as the field's name doesn't also change
mcqs.explanation: A client's code is written against a type, not just a value — string-handling logic breaks the moment the wire type changes, regardless of how equivalent the value looks conceptually. This applies to any field type change, not just currency, and keeping the field name the same doesn't prevent the type-mismatch breakage.
